summary: Prior art converges on one pattern for turning machine text into keys. Run an ordered, deterministic mask pipeline (Sentry's 20-pattern parameterizer, Drain's 1-2 domain regexes, Socorro's address and hash stripping). Key stack traces on in-app module and function, never line numbers (Sentry, Socorro, Crashlytics). Offer several signatures of different granularity, each with a known failure mode (Chromium's three, WER's roughly 500 heuristics, Crashlytics issue and variant). Keep the raw input so keys can be recomputed when the recipe changes (WER re-bucketing, Socorro reprocessing). Learned template miners (Drain, Spell, IPLoM, Logram, Brain) are tuned for millions of frequent lines. Loghub-2.0 shows they handle rare, parameter-heavy templates poorly, and this store is mostly rare errors, so they should not be the primary path. Duplicate-report research says plain full-text retrieval plus categorical fields (REP, Bugzilla FTS) is competitive and neural methods did not help small corpora. FixFlow's own local evidence adds the key warning: error text can mislead. `railway up --ci` always ends in a benign "operation timed out", and alembic raises the identical CommandError for different targets. Keys therefore need tool, phase and command context, plus a verification gate. Also stated: a v0 recipe, with a per-tool table for EAS, Gradle, Alembic, Railway, Docker, pytest, Jest, Vitest and Vite (the Vite and Railway format claims are unverified; see open questions). All engines cited run locally. Sentry, Crashlytics and Elastic cloud are design-only references.

facts.statement: Drain (ICWS 2017) preprocesses each message with simple user-supplied domain regexes (IPs, block IDs), then walks a fixed-depth tree: layer 1 = token count, next layers = leading tokens, then a similarity threshold st picks the log group. Tokens containing digits are routed to a wildcard '*' node to avoid branch explosion. maxChild=100; depth 3-4 and st 0.3-0.5 per dataset. The evaluation needed at most two regexes per dataset.
facts.source: https://jiemingzhu.github.io/pub/pjhe_icws2017.pdf (He, Zhu, Zheng, Lyu, ICWS 2017; text extracted locally from the PDF)

facts.statement: Drain paper Table III accuracy (BGL/HPC/HDFS/Zookeeper/Proxifier): Drain 0.99/0.84/0.99/0.99/0.86; IPLoM 0.99/0.65/0.99/0.99/0.85; Spell 0.98/0.82/0.87/0.99/0.87; SHISO 0.87/0.53/0.93/0.68/0.85; LKE 0.67/0.17/0.57/0.78/0.85. The authors say Spell's LCS-only strategy and LKE's aggressive clustering cause under-partitioning (over-merging), and that avoiding digit tokens in the tree prevents over-partitioning (splitting).

Zhu et al. (ICSE 2019) benchmark 13 parsers on 16 loghub datasets (2000 hand-labelled messages each), using a strict parsing-accuracy metric where partially matched events count as wrong. The same simple preprocessing (IP/number replacement) is applied to every parser. Parameters tuned on small samples do not carry to large volumes: all six top parsers lose accuracy or fluctuate as volume grows (Android drops for all). Drain has the highest mean accuracy and the smallest variance.
facts.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.03509 and text extracted locally from https://arxiv.org/pdf/1811.03509 (v2)

facts.statement: Huawei deployment lessons in the same paper: chose Drain; preprocessing filters common parameters (IP, package name, number, file path); deduplicates messages that become identical after preprocessing; partitions by log header fields (verbosity level, component) before parsing.
facts.source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1811.03509 Sec. on industrial application (text extracted locally)

facts.statement: Loghub-2.0 (ISSTA 2024): 14 datasets, mean 3.6M annotated lines, 15 parsers evaluated. Drain's mean template-grouping score (FGA) falls from 0.75 on the 2k samples to about 0.55 on the full data. Parsers 'struggle to identify infrequent templates (error/fatal levels) and parameter-intensive templates'. 9 of 15 parsers cannot finish all datasets in reasonable time. Good aggregate numbers do not guarantee good parsing of rare or parameter-heavy lines.
facts.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10828 plus text extracted locally from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.10828

facts.statement: Khan, Shin, Bianculli, Briand (ICSE 2022) found earlier parser benchmarks used inconsistent metrics and some wrong ground-truth templates, and report a much less optimistic picture across 14 techniques. A separate 2023 study (arXiv 2308.09003) reports prior studies' average accuracy of about 0.73 versus about 0.2 under a stricter template-accuracy metric; that figure is from a search snippet, not the paper.

Drain3 0.9.11 (released 2022-07-17, MIT, deps cachetools + jsonpickle) is a persistent streaming Drain. It has a regex masking list (mask_with names, default wrapper <...>), sim_th default 0.4, depth default 4, max_children 100, an LRU max_clusters, and extract_parameters(). cluster_id stays stable while a template generalises (e.g. 'user davidoh logged in' becomes 'user <*> logged in'). Persistence: file/Redis/Kafka/memory. It has a parametrize_numeric_tokens switch. Last release is more than 4 years old.

Sentry groups by 'fingerprint first, stack trace next, then exception, with message last'. With a stack trace, grouping uses almost only frames the SDK marks as in-app. Without one it falls back to exception type+value, which Sentry calls 'a lot less reliable because of changing error messages'. The last resort is the message with parameters stripped. AI grouping only merges new issues into existing ones and never splits.

Sentry frame grouping component (newstyle.py) contributes module, filename (lowercased basename), function, and context_line (whitespace-normalised; ignored if over 120 chars) -- not line numbers. Module takes precedence over filename. Language-specific cleanups: Java lambda$/CGLIB/Javassist suffixes become <auto>, Ruby block and ERB suffixes, PHP anonymous classes, JS namespace trimming. Consecutive frames identical on abs_path/package/module/filename/function/lineno/colno are marked non-contributing ('ignored due to recursion'), which is collapse-by-ignoring rather than merging. If no in-app frames exist the app stacktrace is dropped and the system variant is used. NOTE: the docs say revision hashes are stripped from filenames, but the fetched code summary reported no hash removal; the conflict is unresolved.

Sentry's message parameterizer (parameterization.py) applies 20 ordered patterns into one combined regex (first match at each position wins): email, url, hostname (only if the last label is a known TLD), traceparent, uuid, sha1, md5, date (must precede ip because 12:31:12 also matches IPv6), duration, mac_addr, ip (validated with is_valid_ip), swift_txn_id, hex (before random IDs), git_sha, multi_part_random_id, random_id, float, int, quoted_str and bool (only after '='). Placeholders look like <uuid>, <int>. If a callback rejects a candidate (hostname/ip/multi_part_random_id), all patterns are re-run individually so later patterns still get a chance. The normalised message is trimmed to at most two non-empty lines, and the grouping hash is MD5 over the component values.

Sentry customisation layers: fingerprint rules (matcher:glob -> values; first match wins; custom beats built-in; {{ default }} subdivides the default group; matchers include error.type, error.value, message, logger, level, stack.module/function/abs_path/package, tags, app, family) and stack trace rules (+app/-app, +group/-group, ^/v direction, max-frames=N, category matchers, caller|callee syntax). Both affect only new events; existing issues keep their grouping. Variables like {{ error.value }}/{{ message }} over-split when values change; broad fixed names over-merge.

Sentry says new grouping algorithm versions apply only to new events; existing issues keep their old grouping. Minified JavaScript breaks stack-trace grouping unless source maps exist, and the Python SDK skips frames whose local __traceback_hide__ is True.

Mozilla Socorro signature generation for native stacks: (1) start at the first frame matching the sentinel list, (2) skip frames matching the irrelevant list, (3) collapse DLL frames to module name, merging consecutive ones, (4) accumulate frames matching the prefix list and stop at the first non-prefix frame, (5) append ':line' only to frames on a signatures-with-line-numbers list. Parts are pipe-joined. Extra rules prepend 'OOM | <size>', 'shutdownhang', 'stackoverflow', abort message, etc., and the result is whitespace-fixed and truncated. Lists are Python regexes in siglists/; changes go through a Bugzilla bug with example crashes plus a PR, and affected crashes may be reprocessed afterwards. Guidance: platform-variant or post-cause crash-handling symbols go in 'irrelevant'; everything else in 'prefix'.

Socorro CSignatureTool.normalize_frame (rules.py): collapses C++/Rust template args to <T>, drops function arguments and trailing const/&/&& qualifiers, strips Rust ::h<hex> uniqueness hashes, rewrites lambda numbers ::$_N:: to ::$::, removes PGO '[clone .cold.N]' labels, renders function-less frames as file#line (basename), module, or '@offset' with leading zeros stripped. The irrelevant list (about 300 lines, estimate) has entries such as '@0x[0-9a-fA-F]{2,}', compiler helpers, allocation-error handlers and core::/alloc:: internals. Repeated library entries (.dll/.so) are deduplicated.

Chromium crash reports use three signatures with explicit trade-offs: 'Stack Signature' = topmost symbol plus a small callstack hash (readable, but can collide across versions and variance in the stack splits one cause); 'Stack Signature 2' = hash of the whole crashed stack (precise but slight variance defeats bucketing); 'Magic Signature' = heuristic using Chromium-specific knowledge (resists variance, but can give unrelated crashes from different versions the same signature). Buckets are meant to group by 'shared stack frames'.

Windows Error Reporting (SOSP 2009): no ideal algorithm exists for 'one bug, one bucket'. WER uses roughly 500 heuristics (about 100,000 lines of code, roughly one added per week) along two axes: where it runs (client 'labeling' vs server 'classifying') and effect (expanding = more buckets, condensing = fewer). Labels are built from program name/version/timestamp, module name/version/timestamp, module offset and exception code; module_offset alone drives 67.95% of buckets. Programs can override with a developer-assigned stable tag (e.g. assert tag, L15). Upper bound on splitting for Office 2010 ITP: 21.6% (Excel), 17.7% (Outlook), 36.8% (PowerPoint), 28.1% (Word) of reports sit in a second or one-hit bucket. Classifying heuristics are re-run over retained minidumps (kept 6 months) whenever they change, and kernel crashes are re-bucketed.
facts.source: https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~m2nagapp/courses/CS846/1171/papers/glerum_sosp09.pdf (Glerum et al., SOSP 2009; text extracted locally)

facts.statement: Firebase Crashlytics groups events into issues with 'a common point of failure' using stack frames, exception message and error code, and sub-groups events with the same failure point and similar stack into 'variants'. A line-number change does not create a new issue. For new events it first checks for a matching existing issue before applying the new algorithm; regrouping of existing issues is not mentioned.

TraceSim (MaLTeSQuE 2020, JetBrains data): frame weight = local weight 1/i^alpha (position from the top) times global IDF weight (TF deliberately dropped because it ignores order), then Levenshtein-style alignment, with a separate TF-IDF path for stack-overflow traces (recursion). Ablation ROC AUC: full 0.79; without stack-overflow handling 0.78; without local weight 0.76; global-weight IDF contributes the most (+0.10). Baselines: Moroo 0.76, Lerch 0.76, cosine-IDF 0.73, ReBucket 0.70, Levenshtein 0.68, Brodie 0.64, prefix match 0.58. Hyper-parameters were tuned with TPE on a labelled set. 72% of IntelliJ crash reports were duplicates. A 2022 journal extension replaces Levenshtein with global alignment.
facts.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.12590 and text extracted locally from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.12590; extension via https://fis.leuphana.de/en/publications/tracesim-an-alignment-method-for-computing-stack-trace-similarity/

facts.statement: Duplicate bug report detection study (Zhang et al., TOSEM 2023): on a new age- and tracker-debiased benchmark, a simpler technique outperforms recently proposed sophisticated ones on most projects. Bugzilla-style SQL full-text search (FTS, in use at Mozilla) beats several research tools on some projects; REP (2011) is the overall best; deep learning (SABD) only clearly beats REP on projects with very many reports and 'projects with a medium to low volume of historical BRs may not benefit from deep learning-based tools'. The authors recommend simple techniques as mandatory baselines. Prior work cited there found execution information (stack traces) helpful, but few reports contain it.
facts.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.00548 and text extracted locally from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.00548

facts.statement: REP (Sun et al.) scores a pair of reports as a weighted linear combination of 7 features: an extended BM25F over uni-grams and bi-grams of the text, plus five categorical features (product, component, type exact-match; priority and version as inverse distance), with 19 parameters tuned by stochastic gradient descent. DBTM (Nguyen et al., ASE 2012, not Xie et al.) combines BM25F with an LDA-extended topic model by ensemble averaging, with authors claiming up to 20% gain.

Lerch and Mezini (CSMR 2013) detect duplicates from stack traces alone, before any description is written, and report parity with text-based state of the art on Eclipse reports. TraceSim's authors classify their approach as TF-IDF over frames.

Elastic categorize_text: default ml_standard tokenizer filters tokens that could be hexadecimal numbers; a first_line_with_letters filter means only the first meaningful line of multi-line text is used; only the first 100 tokens count; similarity_threshold defaults to 70 (a value of 11 merged distinct groups); categorization_filters are regexes removed before categorising; the algorithm changed completely in 8.3.0 and mixed-version clusters do not work. Needs a running Elasticsearch.

Other parsers: Spell (Du and Li, ICDM 2016, TKDE 2019) is online, longest-common-subsequence based. Logram (Dai et al., TSE 2020) uses n-gram dictionaries, claims 1.8-5.1x speedup over the second-fastest of 5 parsers on 16 datasets, with similar accuracy. Brain (Yu et al., IEEE TSC 2023) uses a bidirectional tree to separate constants from variables (abstract wording from the authors' repo via search; frequency-based per a third-party description). IPLoM is iterative partitioning (KDD 2009). The logpai/logparser benchmark lists ~18 parsers; its README notes Python regex is brittle and pins regex==2022.3.2.

Loghub: 19 datasets, about 90,000 downloads (arXiv 2008.06448). The Loghub-2.0 repo README says the benchmark covers 16 parsers (the paper says 15), including GPU-bound semantic parsers LogPPT and UniParser, and a full run takes over 48 hours with at least 16 GB RAM, 100 GB storage and a GPU.

FixFlow local evidence of a MISLEADING symptom: 'railway up --ci' always ends with 'reqwest error / operation timed out'; that is the log stream dropping, the upload and build succeed, and re-running it double-deploys. The correct remediation is the opposite of what the error text suggests. A text-only key would map this string to the wrong action; the entry must be keyed on tool + command + phase and carry an explicit 'meaning' and 'do not' field.

FixFlow local evidence of an UNDER-DISCRIMINATING symptom: with prod DB at 0046 and rolled-back code that only knows 0045 or lower, alembic raises the identical CommandError for 'head', '0045' and '0044' (alembic 1.18.5). A duplicate revision id also raises on every command including the boot upgrade. The same error text covers different root causes, so the canonical template must be paired with state facts (DB head vs code head, revision ids) that the verification gate re-checks. Alembic docs give message texts for multiple heads ('Multiple head revisions are present for given argument ...', 'Multiple heads are present; please specify the head revision on which the new revision should be based, or perform a merge.', 'Revision X is not a head revision; please ...').

Expo EAS Build troubleshooting: the earliest phase with errors holds the most useful information and later failures often cascade; log lines prefixed [stderr] are not necessarily errors. Documented markers: Android 'Task :app:bundleReleaseJsAndAssets FAILED' (Metro could not bundle JS) and 'Gradle build daemon disappeared unexpectedly' (Node bundler process killed, often a very large bundle). The page gives no log URL format; builds are identified by build page or build ID.

Machine-readable output switches exist for most tools in the stack. Docker buildx: --progress=plain|rawjson (rawjson is 'designed to be read by an external program'), BUILDKIT_PROGRESS env var, --metadata-file (JSON); plain lines look like '#1 [internal] load build definition from Dockerfile' and '#1 DONE 0.1s'. Gradle: --console=plain, --stacktrace, --full-stacktrace, --warning-mode. pytest: --tb=short|line|native|no, -r chars (default fE), summary lines 'FAILED path::test - <message truncated>', --junit-xml. Jest: --json prints only JSON on stdout (other output to stderr), --outputFile, --ci. Vitest: json reporter is Jest-compatible (testResults[].assertionResults[].fullName/failureMessages/location), junit reporter, --outputFile.

The pytest 'short test summary info' line truncates the message (docs example ends 'AssertionError: asser...'). A key derived from that line alone is derived from a truncated message and will differ from the full-traceback key.

Numeric, hex and ID-like tokens are masked in every system reviewed: Drain sends digit-containing tokens to '*'; Sentry masks hex/uuid/sha/int/float/ip/date/duration; Socorro strips '@0x..' offsets, Rust ::h<hex> hashes and lambda numbers; Elastic drops hex-like tokens; Drain3 can mask integers by regex. None of them masks error codes or exception class names. Synthesis across F01, F10, F14, F22.

Sentry's own docs and code, Socorro's mixed regex lists and WER's 500 heuristics all rely on hand-curated lists plus tests rather than learning. Socorro keeps a siglists/ directory and a tests/ directory in the same package. Maintaining the recipe as code with golden fixtures (raw -> expected canonical) is the established practice. The Socorro tests directory exists (verified in the repo listing); the claim that every system tests its lists is inferred.

React Native release builds ship Hermes bytecode / minified bundles; without source maps, frames are bundle offsets rather than module and function names, so frame-based keys degrade to the Sentry-documented minified-JS failure mode. FixFlow's mobile app already uses @sentry/react-native gated on EXPO_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN (CLAUDE.md). Whether source maps are uploaded was not checked.

candidates.name: Ordered deterministic mask pipeline (Sentry-parameterizer / Drain-preprocess style), implemented in-repo
candidates.why: Prior art in F01, F03, F04, F10 and F14 all uses a hand-written, ordered regex list, with order constraints and validated candidates. At tens to hundreds of entries there is nothing to learn from and the cost of error is asymmetric, so a transparent recipe with golden tests beats a learned miner. It works on rare errors, which is where learned miners fail (F05). Recipe v0 appears in the design_implications below. It is a few hundred lines in Node or Python with no dependencies.
candidates.egress_posture: Fully local; no network, no third-party service.
candidates.maturity: Pattern used in production by Sentry (hosted and open source), Mozilla Socorro and Huawei's Drain deployment.
candidates.footprint: One module plus a fixtures file; a few hundred lines.
candidates.agent_access: Exposed as canonicalize(text, tool_hint) in the same CLI or MCP surface that does lookup, so an agent can never store or query an un-canonicalised handle.
candidates.windows_dev_fit: Pure regex; works in Node 24 or Python with no native dependencies. Beware CRLF and backslash paths: normalise to forward slashes first.

candidates.name: Multi-granularity signatures per symptom (Chromium three-signature + Crashlytics issue/variant + WER expanding/condensing)
candidates.why: Every mature crash system keeps several keys with a documented failure mode each: Chromium's stack-hash is precise but brittle, its heuristic key is robust but over-merges (F15). WER separates expanding from condensing heuristics (F16). Crashlytics uses issue then variant (F17). For this store each entry gets handle types H1 exact canonical template hash, H2 tool+error-code or exception class, H3 in-app frame signature, H4 command/phase context, H5 FTS prose. Tune retrieval for precision by letting only H1-H3 hits nominate candidates automatically, with every hit passing the verification gate.
candidates.maturity: Proven at Google, Microsoft and Mozilla scale; we only borrow the shape.
candidates.footprint: A handle table (entry_id, handle_type, key, recipe_version, raw_ref) in whichever engine T-lanes choose.
candidates.agent_access: Lookup returns candidates with per-handle match type so the agent sees why it matched.

candidates.name: Raw copy + canonical form + recipe_version, with re-derivation on recipe change (WER re-bucketing / Socorro reprocessing)
candidates.why: WER re-runs classifying heuristics over retained minidumps and Socorro reprocesses affected crashes (F13, F16), while Sentry only applies new algorithm versions to new events (F12) and leaves old groupings frozen. At a few hundred entries re-derivation is trivially cheap, so the Socorro/WER behaviour is the right one: store the scrubbed raw text, store the canonical text and its recipe_version, and recompute all keys when the recipe changes. This also gives a place to attach invalidation.
candidates.egress_posture: Local; but the raw copy must be secret-scrubbed first because build logs can contain tokens and connection strings (inferred).
candidates.footprint: Two text columns plus a version integer per handle; a recompute command.
candidates.agent_access: CLI: `rederive --all` and a diff report of which keys changed.

candidates.name: Frame-signature keying (Sentry in-app frames + Socorro sentinel/irrelevant/prefix lists), no line numbers
candidates.why: Sentry keys on module+function(+context line), never line numbers, and drops non-app frames and collapses recursion (F09). Socorro adds line numbers only to a hand-listed set and skips known-irrelevant frames (F13, F14). Crashlytics says a line-number change must not create a new issue (F17). Recipe: frames relative to repo root, module+function, top 3 in-app frames as H3, full in-app list kept for scoring, consecutive duplicates collapsed, skip-list for framework frames (starlette, uvicorn, asyncio, _pytest, pluggy, node_modules, react-native internals). Falls back to H1/H2 when frames are minified (F32).
candidates.footprint: A small per-language frame parser (Python traceback, V8/Hermes stack, Gradle/Java), a skip-list file.
candidates.agent_access: canonicalize() returns structured frames as well as text.
candidates.windows_dev_fit: Normalise backslashes and drive letters (C:\Users\... vs /app/...) before keying.

candidates.name: Full-text prose retrieval with categorical filters (Bugzilla FTS / REP-style BM25F + categorical fields)
candidates.why: The best-evidence comparison on duplicate bug reports finds simple retrieval is competitive and that deep learning does not help low-volume projects (F19). REP combines BM25F text with categorical fields, which maps to structured filters here (runtime, slice, tool, phase) (F20). Applies to the fuzzy H5 handle only, and its hits are lower confidence than H1-H3. Engine choice is another lane's (SQLite FTS5 / Postgres FTS / Tantivy-type options all give BM25).
candidates.egress_posture: Local when run on a local engine.
candidates.footprint: One FTS index over canonical text + curated symptom prose.
candidates.windows_dev_fit: Depends on the engine; embedded engines are fine.

candidates.name: Drain / Drain3 as an offline, optional template miner for bulk archived logs
candidates.why: Highest-accuracy and most robust of the classic parsers (F02, F03). Drain3 adds a masking list, parameter extraction and stable cluster ids (F07). It is not the primary path: this store is keyed by rare error events (F05 shows parsers are weakest there), the corpus is far too small for frequency statistics, and its templates mutate as they generalise, so a key derived from a Drain template can drift (F07). Useful only as a one-off discovery tool to find which masks a pile of real CI/build logs needs. Designed for streaming millions of lines; this workload is orders of magnitude smaller.
candidates.egress_posture: Local library; no network use found in its README.
candidates.maturity: Drain3 0.9.11 released 2022-07-17; MIT; classifiers list only Python 3.6/3.7; no release in over 4 years.
candidates.agent_access: Python API only; would need a wrapper.
candidates.windows_dev_fit: Python is not on PATH; a 3.12 interpreter exists but pip install is not allowed in this research, so unverified.
candidates.linux_prod_fit: Fine if Python is present (backend is Python 3.12).

candidates.name: Spell, IPLoM, Logram, Brain (other classical log parsers)
candidates.why: Spell (online LCS), IPLoM (iterative partitioning), Logram (n-gram dictionaries, speed), Brain (bidirectional tree, frequency analysis) are all optimised for high-volume streams and benchmarked on millions of lines (F23, F24). Spell and LKE are noted as prone to under-partitioning (F02). Nothing they add justifies another dependency when masking is done by hand. Design notes worth keeping: group by log header fields first (F04), and warn that learned parameters do not transfer between small and large samples (F03).

candidates.name: LLM / semantic log parsers (LogPPT, UniParser, DivLog)
candidates.why: Loghub-2.0 notes they need GPUs and separate environments (F24) and show weaker grouping despite better constant/variable separation (F05). Using a hosted LLM on defect text would also break the no-egress rule. Overkill for tens to hundreds of entries.
candidates.egress_posture: Local needs a GPU; hosted variants send text to a third party (disqualified).

candidates.name: Sentry (hosted) grouping, fingerprint rules and stack trace rules
candidates.why: Best-documented grouping design: priority order fingerprint > stack > exception > message (F08), frame component recipe (F09), parameterizer (F10), {{ default }} subdivision and stack-trace rules (F11). Hosted Sentry receives stack traces and messages and so cannot hold the store's defect data. Self-hosting Sentry is a large multi-service stack (inferred; not verified here), wrong for one developer. FixFlow's mobile app already sends crashes to Sentry (CLAUDE.md), which is a separate owner decision and is not the knowledge store.
candidates.egress_posture: Hosted: sends data to a third party (disqualified for the store). Self-hosted: local but heavy.
candidates.footprint: n/a for the store; design reference only.

candidates.name: Mozilla Socorro signature generator (siggen) ideas / library
candidates.why: The sentinel -> irrelevant -> prefix -> line-number list design, plus a change process (bug with examples, PR, reprocess) maps directly onto a curated frame skip-list with a changelog (F13, F14). The library (socorro.signature / siggen) was not inspected for license or standalone installability, and it is aimed at C/C++/Rust/Java native crashes. Adopt the structure, not the code.
candidates.maturity: Production at Mozilla for years; actively maintained per the docs.
candidates.footprint: Python package within a larger repo.

candidates.name: TraceSim / ReBucket-style stack similarity scoring
candidates.why: Best published stack-trace similarity (ROC AUC 0.79 vs 0.58 prefix-match baseline, F18), but the largest gain (+0.10) comes from IDF over a large frame corpus, which a few hundred entries cannot supply. Designed for deduplicating millions of crash reports. Revisit only if the number of stored frame lists passes a few hundred; until then H3 exact top-frames plus FTS is enough. Keep position-weighted idea (1/i^alpha) as a cheap tie-breaker.
candidates.maturity: 2020 workshop paper plus 2022 journal extension; implementation licence not checked.

candidates.name: Neural crash/duplicate-report methods (DeepCrash, dedupT, DeepLSH, SABD)
candidates.why: Need training data and GPUs, tuned thresholds (DeepCrash needs manual threshold tuning, per a 2025 paper). F19 finds no benefit for low-volume corpora and that simple baselines win on most projects. No evidence in this lane that they work on build-tool output. I did not read the DeepCrash paper directly.
candidates.egress_posture: Local training possible, but not warranted.

candidates.name: Elasticsearch categorize_text aggregation
candidates.why: Interesting design points: hex-token filtering, first meaningful line only, 100-token cap, similarity threshold 70 (F22). Requires a running Elasticsearch cluster; its categorisation algorithm was replaced wholesale in 8.3.0, so category identity is unstable across versions. Heavy to run for one developer and tuned for log volumes this store never reaches.
candidates.egress_posture: Self-hosted is local, but a managed offering would egress.
candidates.maturity: Mature product; this feature's algorithm changed in 8.3.0.

candidates.name: Proposed canonicalisation recipe v0 (composite of the above)
candidates.why: Layering: L0 raw -> scrub -> L1 normalise text -> L2 per-tool extraction -> L3 mask -> L4 handles. L0: strip ANSI escapes and carriage-return progress redraws, convert CRLF and backslashes to '/', redact secrets (tokens, DATABASE_URL, Authorization, anything matching key=value secrets) before storing. L1 per-tool 'which lines count': first error-phase block, not last (EAS: earliest failing phase, F27); keep only the first meaningful 1-2 lines of the message (Sentry trims to 2, Elastic first line with letters, F10/F22). L3 mask order (Sentry constraints): url/email -> uuid -> sha/git-sha/md5 -> ISO or clock timestamp and durations (before ip) -> ip(validated) -> hex (0x..., addresses) -> long random-looking ids/EAS build ids -> repo-absolute paths rewritten to repo-relative and user/temp prefixes (C:/Users/<u>/..., /tmp/pytest-of-*/pytest-N, /app/..) to <path> prefix while KEEPING the file basename -> line:col suffixes (:123:45) -> float -> int, with quoted strings masked only after '='. DO NOT mask: exception/class names, error codes (TS2345, E0432, ruff rule ids, HTTP status), Gradle task paths (:app:bundleReleaseJsAndAssets), alembic revision ids in the template key (keep them as separate slot values), flag and env names, tool and package names, and version numbers of the tool. Keep every masked value as ordered slots beside the template (Drain3 extract_parameters style) so the verification gate can re-check them. Handles: H1 sha256(recipe_version|tool|canonical_first_lines), H2 tool + phase + code/exception class, H3 top 3 in-app frames as module::function, H4 command string with args masked (e.g. 'railway up --ci' + cwd class backend/ vs root), H5 FTS over canonical + curated prose. Bias to splitting (WER: splitting is the common failure; here a miss is cheap). Golden fixtures for every tool; a recipe change bumps recipe_version and triggers rederive.
candidates.egress_posture: Local; scrub step is what keeps secrets out of the stored raw copy.
candidates.maturity: New composite; every element has precedent, the composite is untested on FixFlow logs.
candidates.agent_access: One entry point exposed through the CLI or MCP.
candidates.windows_dev_fit: Path normalisation is required (backslashes, drive letters, CRLF, ANSI from Windows terminals).

candidates.name: Per-tool adapters preferring structured output (EAS, Gradle, Alembic, Railway CLI, Docker, pytest, Jest, Vitest, Vite)
candidates.why: Prefer the machine-readable mode where the tool has one: pytest --junit-xml or the full traceback (not the truncated short summary, F29), Jest --json and Vitest --reporter=json (fullName, failureMessages, F28), Docker --progress=plain or rawjson plus --metadata-file (F28), Gradle --console=plain with --stacktrace (F28). Key per tool: pytest = nodeid without parametrize suffix + exception class + masked first assertion line; Jest/Vitest = fullName + failure message first line masked; Docker = failing Dockerfile instruction text (not step number '#12') + exit code; Gradle = failed task path + first 'What went wrong' line (format inferred from experience, not fetched); EAS = failing phase name + Gradle task or Metro marker (F27), build id masked; Alembic = exception class + message template with revision ids as slots (F26); Railway CLI = command + phase + exit state, because the text alone misleads (F25); Vite = rollup/esbuild error message template with module id as slot (error format not verified in this lane). EAS and Railway CLI have no verified machine-readable log format in this lane.
candidates.maturity: Documented flags exist for pytest, Jest, Vitest, Docker, Gradle; EAS, Railway, Vite and Alembic formats not verified.
candidates.footprint: Roughly 9 small adapters; the first three (pytest, Jest/Vitest, Alembic) cover the most-run tools.
candidates.agent_access: Adapter chosen by tool_hint argument; an unknown tool falls through to the generic mask pipeline.
candidates.windows_dev_fit: Fine; Windows terminals add ANSI and CRLF.

design_implications.claim: Use a deterministic, ordered, human-readable mask pipeline as the canonicaliser, not a learned log-template miner. Mask order matters (timestamps before IPs, hex before random IDs, validate IP/hostname candidates). Keep error codes, exception class names, task paths and file basenames unmasked. The corpus is tens to hundreds of entries, error events are rare, and learned parsers are weakest exactly on rare, parameter-heavy lines.

Keep the (secret-scrubbed) raw text beside the canonical form and record recipe_version on every derived key. A recipe change must trigger re-derivation of all handles. WER and Socorro re-process stored raw data when rules change; Sentry's freeze-old-groups approach is a poor fit at this size. Without the raw copy a recipe fix cannot be applied retroactively.

Give each entry several handles of different granularity, each with a stated failure mode: H1 exact canonical-template hash (precise, brittle), H2 tool + phase + error code/exception class (robust, may over-merge), H3 top-3 in-app frame signature, H4 command-and-context handle, H5 full-text prose. Only H1-H3 should surface automatic candidates; H5 returns 'maybe' results. All hits pass the verification gate. This mirrors Chromium's three signatures and Crashlytics' issue/variant levels.

Key stack traces on in-app module::function, never line numbers, with repo-relative paths, consecutive-duplicate frame collapse (recursion), and a curated, changelogged skip-list for framework frames (the Socorro irrelevant/prefix pattern and Sentry's stack trace rules). Keep the full in-app list for scoring. If frames are minified (Hermes release builds without source maps), fall back to H1/H2 rather than keying on bundle offsets.

Symptom text alone is an unreliable key and is sometimes dangerous. FixFlow's own traps show two failure shapes: a benign-looking-failure message that must NOT trigger a retry (railway up --ci 'operation timed out'), and one identical alembic CommandError produced by different states. Entries need tool + phase + command context, a 'meaning of this symptom' field including 'misleading' flags, and state predicates (DB head vs code head) in the verification gate. Sentry's own doc ranks message-only grouping as the least reliable tier.

Bias every default toward splitting (more, narrower keys). WER measured 17-37% of Office reports landing in a second or one-hit bucket, so splitting is the common failure of conservative keys, and the store tolerates it because a miss is cheap. Merging distinct bugs is the dangerous direction. Tune retrieval to be strict by default, and never let a loose handle (H4, H5) auto-nominate.

For the fuzzy, human-worded handle use plain BM25-style full-text retrieval plus structured filters (runtime, slice, tool, phase), the REP shape. Do not plan embeddings or neural similarity. The duplicate-report benchmark finds simple baselines win on most projects and deep learning does not help low-volume corpora.

Per-tool adapters should request structured output where it exists (pytest --junit-xml, Jest/Vitest json reporters, Docker --progress=plain/rawjson, Gradle --console=plain) and key on the earliest failing phase. For Docker key on the instruction text rather than the '#N' step number; for pytest do not key on the truncated short-summary line. Start with pytest, Jest/Vitest and Alembic adapters; EAS, Railway and Vite adapters need real log samples first.

The recipe is code with golden fixtures: raw sample -> expected canonical text and handles, one fixture per tool, starting from FixFlow's own real traps (railway timeout, alembic head mismatch, EAS gradle failures). A recipe change must pass all fixtures or bump recipe_version intentionally. This keeps the maintenance burden to a list and a test file for a one-person team.

Scrub secrets and personal paths before storing the raw copy (tokens, DATABASE_URL, Authorization headers, user profile paths). Build and deploy logs routinely contain them; the store must not become a secret archive, and the raw copy is what survives into backups and git. This is inferred from the data-stays-local constraint rather than from a cited source.

Defer stack-similarity scoring (TraceSim/ReBucket style) until frame corpora reach a few hundred entries. Its main benefit comes from IDF over many traces, which a small store lacks; a hand-curated skip-list is the equivalent here. A cheap position weight (1/i^alpha) can break ties between H3 candidates.

rejected_paths.what: Learned template miners (Drain/Drain3, Spell, IPLoM, Logram, Brain) as the primary canonicaliser
rejected_paths.why: Built for frequent lines in millions-line streams; templates drift as they generalise (F07); Loghub-2.0 shows they struggle with infrequent and parameter-heavy templates (F05); parameters tuned on small samples do not transfer (F03). A masked-regex recipe is simpler, deterministic and explainable. Drain3 stays an optional offline discovery aid.

rejected_paths.what: Hosted Sentry, Crashlytics or any hosted grouping service as the store
rejected_paths.why: They receive stack traces and messages, so they are disqualified for production use by the no-third-party-egress rule. Cited for design only.

rejected_paths.what: Self-hosted Sentry or Elasticsearch categorize_text for grouping
rejected_paths.why: Heavy services for one developer, aimed at crash and log volumes far above this workload. The Elastic algorithm was replaced wholesale in 8.3.0 (F22). The Sentry self-hosting footprint was not verified here.

rejected_paths.what: Neural stack-trace and duplicate-report models (DeepCrash, dedupT, DeepLSH, SABD) and LLM parsers (LogPPT, UniParser)
rejected_paths.why: Need training data and GPUs; evidence says they do not help low-volume corpora (F19); hosted LLM variants would send defect text to a third party.

rejected_paths.what: Keying on a hash of raw error text, or on line numbers
rejected_paths.why: Raw text carries timestamps, ids, paths and counts, so every instance gets a different key. Line numbers shift on every edit and Sentry, Socorro and Crashlytics all avoid them as default keys (F09, F13, F17).

rejected_paths.what: Keying on error text alone for build/deploy traps
rejected_paths.why: FixFlow's own traps: the railway timeout is benign and re-running double-deploys (F25), and alembic raises one identical CommandError for several different targets and states (F26).

rejected_paths.what: Freezing old keys when the recipe changes (Sentry's new-events-only model)
rejected_paths.why: Suits a hosted service with millions of events. At this scale, re-deriving from the raw copy is cheap and avoids two recipe generations living side by side.

open_questions: Per-tool real-output samples are missing: collect 3-5 real raw logs per tool from FixFlow history (EAS, Gradle, Railway CLI, Docker, Vite) and run the v0 recipe over them to see which masks over- or under-fire. Railway CLI and Vite error formats, and Gradle's 'What went wrong' block, were not verified from primary docs in this lane.

Does the EAS Build log expose phases as machine-readable fields (eas build:view --json, build logs URL)? Not confirmed here; the troubleshooting page only names phases in prose and a 404 occurred on the eas-json reference URL.
Are Sentry source maps for the Hermes release bundle uploaded for the technician app? If not, mobile stack frames are bundle offsets and the H3 frame handle is useless for mobile crashes.

What fraction of stored entries will have stack traces at all versus build/deploy text or purely semantic defects? The recipe invests in frames; if most entries are semantic/behavioural, the H2/H4/H5 handles carry the weight.
Socorro's siggen library: licence, standalone installability and Python version support were not checked; only the design was read.
TraceSim reference implementation: licence and language were not verified (linked as reference [3] in the paper).

The Sentry docs claim filename hash normalisation but the fetched grouping code summary showed none; the discrepancy is unresolved and might be old documentation, a different strategy version, or a WebFetch summarisation error.
WER's '40% of reports in multiple buckets, 4% merged' figure came from a search snippet about a 2010 talk, not the SOSP paper; only Figure 16's 17.7%-36.8% range is verified.
Khan et al. (ICSE 2022) actual numbers were not obtained; the 0.73 vs 0.2 figure comes from a different 2023 study via a search snippet.

How should the canonicaliser treat chained exceptions (Python 'During handling... another exception occurred', JS error.cause)? Sentry groups on the chain; no verified source was read for the exact rule.

Windows vs Linux log divergence: the same failure on the Windows dev box and a Linux CI/prod produces different paths, line endings and sometimes different message wording. The path normalisation step handles paths; message wording divergence is untested.

WebFetch summarises through a small model and may paraphrase inexactly. Sentry and Socorro source facts rest on WebFetch summaries of the raw files and are less direct.
One download was made outside WebFetch: curl saved https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.12590 (TraceSim, 299 KB) into the scratchpad. It was only text-extracted, never executed. Not repeated for other papers.
